primer.text: From Measuring Rates you already know the four levers that speed reactions up. This note goes underneath the lever names to particle collision theory, explaining each effect through the number and energy of collisions. One small temperature step turns out to matter far more than its size suggests.

lessons.title: Collision theory for concentration and pressure
lessons.opening: Reactions happen when particles collide, and only some collisions succeed. This lesson uses that rule to explain why crowding particles together, in solution or in gas, makes chemistry run faster.
keyPoints: Increasing the number of successful collisions means a greater proportion of particles form products.
A higher concentration puts more reactant particles into the same volume.
More particles in a given volume cause more collisions per second, so the rate increases.
Raising the pressure squeezes the same number of gas particles into a smaller volume.
Doubling the number of particles doubles the collisions per second, so collisions are proportional to particle count.

low.restatement: Crowd more particles into the same space and they bump into each other more often, so more reactions happen every second. The same trick works for gases by squeezing them into less room.
low.analogy: It is like shoppers in a busy market: pack more of them into one street and bumping into friends becomes far more likely.
low.examPointer: Answer with the chain: more particles in the same volume, more collisions, faster rate.

medium.restatement: Higher concentration means more reactant particles in a given volume, causing more collisions per second and therefore more frequent successful collisions. Higher pressure does the same for gases by holding the same number of particles in a smaller volume.
medium.analogy: A crowded commuter train produces far more shoulder bumps per minute than a nearly empty one, even though the passengers are identical.
medium.examPointer: Include the phrase more frequent and successful collisions per second when explaining the faster rate.

check.stem: Why does doubling the concentration roughly double the collision count?

options.text: Because collisions per second are proportional to the number of particles present
options.explanation: Twice the particles in the same volume meet twice as often.

options.text: Because each particle then moves faster
options.explanation: Concentration changes crowding, not particle speed.

options.text: Because the volume doubles too
options.explanation: The volume stays the same; the population doubles.

options.text: Because the acid becomes stronger chemically
options.explanation: The explanation is mechanical crowding, not chemical strength.

check.stem: How does increased pressure speed up a gaseous reaction?

options.text: The same number of particles is forced into a smaller volume, so collisions become more frequent
options.explanation: Squeezing the crowd raises the bump rate per second.

options.text: Pressure adds energy to each particle
options.explanation: Pressure changes spacing; energy belongs to the temperature story.

options.text: Pressure creates extra particles
options.explanation: The particle count is unchanged.

options.text: Pressure only affects liquids
options.explanation: Pressure effects are quoted for gases in this topic.

check.stem: What converts an ordinary collision into a successful one?

options.text: Enough energy and the right arrangement, so product molecules form
options.explanation: Only a proportion of collisions carry what it takes to react.

options.text: The particles colliding head-on at any speed
options.explanation: Direction alone is not enough without the energy requirement.

options.text: The particles sticking together permanently
options.explanation: Products form and separate; permanent sticking is not the rule.

options.text: The presence of a catalyst in every collision
options.explanation: Catalysts are absent in most explained reactions here.

check.stem: A flask of gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. What happens to the rate?

options.text: It increases because the particle crowding and collision count rise
options.explanation: Half the volume means twice the crowding, so collisions per second rise.

options.text: It decreases because particles have less room to move
options.explanation: Less room means more meetings, not fewer.

options.text: It stays the same because particle count is fixed
options.explanation: Count is fixed but crowding is not.

options.text: It doubles only if a catalyst is added
options.explanation: No catalyst is needed for the pressure effect.

check.stem: Which chain of reasoning correctly explains a faster rate at higher concentration?

options.text: More particles per volume, more collisions per second, more successful collisions, faster rate
options.explanation: Each link follows from the previous one and ends at the rate.

options.text: Faster rate, more collisions, more particles, higher concentration
options.explanation: The chain runs backwards from the outcome.

options.text: Higher concentration, slower particles, fewer collisions, faster rate
options.explanation: Speed and count are mixed up mid-chain.

options.text: More particles, fewer collisions, faster rate
options.explanation: The middle link contradicts crowding.

lessons.title: Collision theory for temperature and surface area
sourceHeadings: How increasing the surface area affects rate
lessons.opening: Heat does two jobs at once: particles move faster and collide more often, and each collision arrives with more energy. This lesson separates those jobs and adds the exposure effect of powdered solids.
keyPoints: Increasing the temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so collisions become more frequent and successful.
A small rise in temperature causes a large increase in rate.
For aqueous and gaseous systems, every 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate of reaction.
Increasing the surface area exposes more particles of a solid to the other reactant.
Doubling the surface area doubles the number of collisions per second.

low.restatement: Warmer particles dash about faster, so they meet more often and hit harder, which lifts the rate steeply. Chopping a solid into smaller pieces uncovers more of its particles for the other reactant to strike.
low.analogy: Heating a crowd makes everyone jog instead of stroll, so shoulders bump far more; powdering a sugar cube spreads its grains through the tea for faster dissolving.
low.examPointer: For temperature, mention both collision frequency and collision energy; for surface area, mention exposed particles.

medium.restatement: Higher temperature raises the kinetic energy of particles, causing more collisions per second and more frequent successful collisions, so a 10 °C rise can roughly double the rate. Greater surface area places more solid particles where the other reactant can reach them, again raising the collision count.
medium.analogy: A hotter dance floor has dancers moving faster and colliding with more force, while a broken-up dance card lets twice as many partners meet.
medium.examPointer: Quote the 10 °C doubling rule as a rule of thumb, and credit temperature as the more powerful of the two effects.

check.stem: Why does a 10 °C rise have such a large effect on rate?

options.text: Because collisions become both more frequent and more energetic
options.explanation: The two effects combine, with the energy gain doing the greater work.

options.text: Because particles double in size
options.explanation: Particle size does not change with temperature.

options.text: Because the concentration rises with temperature
options.explanation: Concentration is a separate factor.

options.text: Because the reaction switches to a faster pathway
options.explanation: No new pathway appears; the same one runs faster.

check.stem: What does the rough rule of thumb state for aqueous and gaseous systems?

options.text: Every 10 °C increase in temperature approximately doubles the rate
options.explanation: The stated rule of thumb links a 10 °C step to a doubling of rate.

options.text: Every 10 °C increase halves the rate
options.explanation: Heating speeds reactions; the rule says doubles.

options.text: Every 1 °C increase doubles the rate
options.explanation: The doubling belongs to a 10 °C step.

options.text: Rate is unaffected below 50 °C
options.explanation: No threshold appears in the rule.

check.stem: Why does powdering a solid reactant speed up the reaction?

options.text: More solid particles are exposed to the other reactant, so collisions per second increase
options.explanation: Exposure is the whole story; the powder meets the solution everywhere at once.

options.text: Powder particles move faster than lumps
options.explanation: Speed of particles is a temperature effect, not a surface effect.

options.text: Powdering raises the concentration of the solution
options.explanation: The solid is not part of the solution concentration.

options.text: Powder lowers the activation energy
options.explanation: Only catalysts lower the energy barrier.

check.stem: A student claims doubling the surface area doubles the amount of product formed. What is the correction?

options.text: Doubling the surface area doubles the collision count, not the final product amount
options.explanation: The plateau is fixed by the starting quantities; only the pace changes.

options.text: The claim is correct because rate and yield are identical
options.explanation: Rate and yield are different quantities.

options.text: Doubling the surface area halves the product
options.explanation: No such penalty exists.

options.text: Product amount depends on the powder colour
options.explanation: Colour is irrelevant to yield.

check.stem: Which factor affects reaction rate by increasing both the number and the energy of collisions?

options.text: Temperature
options.explanation: Heat raises particle speed, so collisions come more often and hit harder.

options.text: Surface area
options.explanation: Surface area changes only the number of exposed collision sites.

options.text: Concentration
options.explanation: Concentration changes crowding, not particle energy.

options.text: A catalyst
options.explanation: A catalyst changes the energy barrier, not the particle energies.

glossary.definition: The explanation of reaction rates in terms of the frequency and energy of particle collisions.
The amount of dissolved reactant in a given volume of solution.
A collision between reactant particles that forms product molecules.
The energy of moving particles, which rises with temperature.
The amount of solid surface available for collisions, increased by powdering a solid.

workedExample.prompt: a) Use collision theory to explain why increasing the concentration of a solution increases the rate of reaction. b) Why does a 10 °C rise in temperature approximately double the rate for aqueous and gaseous systems? c) Why does powdering a solid reactant increase the rate of reaction?
steps: a) A higher concentration means more reactant particles in the same volume, so there are more collisions per second and therefore more frequent successful collisions — the rate increases.

b) Higher temperature gives the particles more kinetic energy, so collisions become both more frequent and more energetic; that is why a small rise causes a large increase, and the rule of thumb is that every 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate.
c) Powdering the solid exposes more of its particles to the other reactant, so more collisions occur each second and the rate rises.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) More particles per volume → more frequent successful collisions. b) More kinetic energy → more frequent and more energetic collisions (≈ doubling per 10 °C). c) More exposed particles → more collisions.
